prompt:
Big-O is defined by a quantified statement:

```formula
f(n) = O(g(n))   iff
∃c > 0 ∃n_0 ∀n ≥ n_0 : f(n) ≤ c · g(n)
where
f(n), g(n): functions of the input size n
n: the input size, a natural number
c: a positive constant multiplier
n_0: a non-negative integer threshold input size
O(g(n)): "Big-O of g": grows no faster than a constant times g
∃: there exists at least one
∀: for all
≤: is at most
·: multiplied by
:: "such that"
≥: at least
>: greater than
In words: some constant c and threshold n_0 make f(n) at most c times g(n) for every n from n_0 on.
```

To prove f is **not** O(g), what must you show? Assume eventually nonnegative functions on natural-number inputs.

*Symbols: ∀ means "for all"; ∃ means "there exists at least one".*

options.text: there exists c is greater than 0 ∃n₀ for every integer n at least n₀ : f(n) is greater than c times g(n)
options.explanation: This is a different statement, not the negation. For f(n) equals g(n) equals n, choosing c equals 1/2 and n₀ equals 1 makes it true (n is greater than n/2 for every integer n at least 1) even though f is O(g).

options.text: for every c is greater than 0 ∀n₀ for every integer n at least n₀ : f(n) is greater than c times g(n)
options.explanation: The for every n should become there exists n. You only need one large n per choice of c and n₀, not every n.

options.text: for every c is greater than 0 ∀n₀ there exists n is at least n₀ : f(n) is greater than c times g(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Each quantifier flips (there exists implies for every, there exists implies for every, for every implies there exists ) and the inequality ≤ becomes >.

options.text: there exists n : f(n) is greater than g(n)
options.explanation: One point where f exceeds g says nothing about asymptotic growth; constants and thresholds are ignored.

workedExample:
Push ¬ through left to right, flipping each quantifier, then negate the inequality:

```formula
¬∃c ∃n_0 ∀n ≥ n_0 : f ≤ c · g
  ≡ ∀c ¬∃n_0 ∀n ≥ n_0 : f ≤ c · g
  ≡ ∀c ∀n_0 ¬∀n ≥ n_0 : f ≤ c · g
  ≡ ∀c ∀n_0 ∃n ≥ n_0 : ¬(f ≤ c · g)
  ≡ ∀c ∀n_0 ∃n ≥ n_0 : f > c · g
where
f, g: short for f(n) and g(n), the two functions of the input size n
n: the input size, a natural number
c: a positive constant multiplier (c > 0 throughout)
n_0: a non-negative integer threshold input size
∃: there exists at least one
∀: for all
¬: NOT
≤, >: is at most, is greater than
·: multiplied by
:: "such that"
≡: is logically equivalent to
≥: at least
In words: f is not O(g) when, for every constant c and every threshold n_0, there is some n at or beyond n_0 where f(n) is bigger than c times g(n).
```

Example: n squared is not O(n). Given any c and n₀, choose a large enough n:

```formula
n = max(n_0, ⌊c⌋ + 1)
n^2 = n · n > c · n
where
n: the input size you choose
n_0: the non-negative integer threshold you were given
c: the positive constant you were given
max(a, b): the larger of a and b
⌊c⌋: c rounded down to a whole number, so ⌊c⌋ + 1 > c
·: multiplied by
>: greater than
⌊: floor: round down to the nearest integer
⌋: closes the floor operation
In words: pick n at least n_0 and bigger than c; then n² = n · n is bigger than c · n.
```
